name: Chemical peels (TCA, Jessner)

lead: A medium-depth chemical peel removes damaged upper skin layers so fresher, smoother skin forms. Clinicians use trichloroacetic acid (TCA), often after Jessner's solution, for photoaged skin, fine wrinkles, melasma and acne scars.

TCA denatures proteins in the skin, causing a controlled injury and shedding followed by regeneration. In the Jessner plus TCA technique, Jessner's solution (a keratolytic mix) is applied first so TCA acts more evenly; glycolic acid has also been used as a pre-treatment. Published studies are mostly small clinical series, comparisons and some randomised trials.

paras: Peels are performed by a medical provider, with skin often prepared beforehand, then followed by a recovery period of redness and peeling. A small number of forum members have discussed doing TCA peels at home.

Reported risks include prolonged redness, photosensitivity, pigment changes, milia, atrophy and scarring. General references state that deeper peels bring more complications and that DIY kits carry a higher risk of injury and scarring. Tretinoin pre-treatment has been shown in one trial to accelerate healing.

angle.text: Medium-depth peels with TCA, Jessner's solution or glycolic acid remove damaged top layers so skin renews, aiming for a smoother, more even complexion with less pigment and fewer fine lines. They are an established clinician-performed procedure; DIY versions circulate in appearance forums.

lead: Medium-depth chemical peels use trichloroacetic acid (TCA), sometimes after Jessner's solution or glycolic acid, to produce a controlled injury to the epidermis and upper dermis. As the injured layers shed and regenerate over days to weeks, skin can look smoother and more even. They are used in dermatology for photoaged skin, actinic keratoses, fine wrinkles, pigmentary disorders such as melasma, benign pigmented lesions and atrophic acne scars, which are the skin-quality problems people in appearance communities most often want fixed.[1][2][3][4][5]

The combination technique has a documented history. A 1989 paper described the Jessner's plus TCA peel as a medium-depth peel for photoaging, actinic keratoses and rhytides; a 1994 paper described a glycolic acid plus TCA variant intended to make penetration more predictable; and a 1999 paper described a standardised TCA-based blue peel with depth control.[1][6][7] Jessner's solution is named for the dermatologist Max Jessner, and TCA itself was first reported by Jean-Baptiste Dumas in 1839.[8][9]

General references state that medium-depth peels must be performed by a medical provider, that deeper peels bring more complications, and that DIY kits carry a higher risk of injury and scarring.[5] The published literature consists of small clinical series, comparative studies, some randomised trials, a systematic review of peels in melasma and a handful of registered trials.[10][11][12][13][14]

paras: Peels are classed by depth: light peels use alpha- or beta-hydroxy acids, medium peels use TCA, and deep peels have historically used phenol with croton oil.[5] A 2019 review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology covers superficial and medium-depth peels, and a 2024 update in Dermatologic Clinics reviews new concepts in the field.[15][16]

TCA peels are performed in an office or outpatient setting, patients often feel warmth or burning, and sedation or topical anaesthetic is sometimes used.[5][17] In the Jessner's plus TCA technique, Jessner's solution is applied before TCA to prepare the skin; the 1994 glycolic acid variant used glycolic acid in the same pre-treatment role, and the 1999 blue peel is a standardised variant intended to control depth.[1][6][7] A review of the combination describes it as an enhanced medium-depth peel for photoaged skin.[18]

Jessner's solution combines salicylic acid, resorcinol and lactic acid in ethanol; Jessner lowered the resorcinol concentration because it caused contact dermatitis and discoloration, and versions with TCA in place of resorcinol also exist.[8] The same pre-treatment idea appears with retinoic acid peels, where Jessner's solution is applied first to help penetration.[5]

Photoaging and wrinkles: the Jessner's plus TCA peel was introduced for sun-damaged skin, actinic keratoses and fine wrinkles.[1][18] Acne scars: a study of combination therapy used subcision, microneedling and a 15 percent TCA peel in 50 patients with atrophic scars.[3] Acne reviews list chemical peels among procedural options for scarring.[19]

Pigment: a comparative study examined TCA peel with and without topical ascorbic acid in melasma, and a 2004 paper described a focal TCA method for benign pigmented lesions in dark-skinned patients.[20][4] A 2024 review describes peels in melasma as additional or maintenance therapy, and a 2024 systematic review of 24 studies and 1,075 patients reported peels as safe and effective for melasma, with glycolic acid rated safest and most effective; meta-analysis was not possible because of heterogeneity.[11][10] A 2025 Latin American consensus lists peels among procedural options for melasma alongside lasers and microneedling, and emphasises photoprotection and individualised therapy.[21][22]

Chemical peels date to the second half of the nineteenth century, when Austrian dermatologist Ferdinand Ritter von Hebra used phenol, croton oil and nitric acid for freckles and skin irregularities. Phenol-croton oil peeling was used discreetly by Hollywood stars in the 1920s and entered mainstream practice in the 1960s through Thomas Baker and Howard Gordon.[5]

Trichloroacetic acid was reported by Jean-Baptiste Dumas in 1839 and is used in laboratories to precipitate proteins as well as in peels and wart treatment.[9] Max Jessner (born 1887 in Stolp) was a German dermatologist who later settled in New York; the solution named for him is used for thickened skin lesions.[8] The Jessner's plus TCA method was published in 1989, tretinoin pre-treatment was trialled in 1991, and the glycolic acid and blue peel variants followed in 1994 and 1999.[1][2][6][7]

General references list photosensitivity, prolonged redness, pigment changes, milia, skin atrophy, texture changes and scarring as risks, and state that professional peels and low-concentration DIY kits can both cause injury and scarring.[5] European regulators classify pure trichloroacetic acid as causing severe skin burns and eye damage, which is why handling guidance describes it as a hazardous chemical.[9]

A trial found that tretinoin pre-treatment accelerated healing after a TCA peel.[2] A 2000 comparison examined two topical anaesthetic creams for pain relief in medium-depth peeling.[17] A Latin American consensus notes melasma is relapsing and most frequent in darker phototypes, and recommends rigorous photoprotection and treatment tailored to skin sensitivity and prior treatments.[21]

Medium-depth peels are discussed in hardmaxxing contexts as clinic-based options for pigment, acne scars and texture, and often alongside microneedling, lasers and retinoids. Looksmax.org contains at least one thread in which members ask who has done a DIY TCA peel, and another in which a member with long-standing acne describes chemical peels as the first thing that worked for them; those threads supply personal accounts rather than data and are not cited here.

A double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised study in 16 men (mean age 67) with actinically damaged skin applied 0.1 percent tretinoin and placebo to opposite sides for 14 days before a TCA peel to assess healing.[2] Case series and comparative studies cover Jessner plus TCA for photoaging, glycolic acid plus TCA, and TCA in melasma and acne scars.[1][3][6][20]

Registered trials include a completed phase 4 comparison of Jessner's solution versus TCA for melasma (2008, n=19), a completed phase 4 study of 15 percent TCA for hand lentigines (2023, n=20), a phase 4 trial combining TCA with microdermabrasion for melasma (2021, n=60, status unknown), a completed phase 2 comparison of intralesional saline versus 35 percent TCA for atrophic acne scars (2023, n=126), a completed phase 3 study of medium-depth peel with or without botulinum toxin pretreatment for lateral canthal wrinkles (2011, n=26), a phase 4 comparison of laser versus 20 percent TCA for keratosis pilaris (2021, n=20) and an ongoing comparison of TCA peel with fractional laser (2025, n=120).[12][13][14][23][24][25][26] A 2023 paper used high-frequency ultrasound to monitor anti-aging skin therapy.[27]
